title: Harbor Adds Docker Sandboxes to Run Reproducible AI Agent Evals in Isolated MicroVMs
gist: Docker added Docker Sandboxes support to the open-source Harbor agent-eval framework so each evaluation task runs in its own microVM (tested at 64 concurrent cloud tasks), addressing untrusted code and reward hacking concerns; the article notes no benchmark data on cost, latency or variance and that stable release arrives October 23.

insights.claim: Evaluating a coding agent means letting it install packages, edit files and run commands thousands of times, which Docker describes as running untrusted, AI-written code at scale.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Eval infrastructure is a security surface, driving demand for sandboxing.
insights.locator: Evaluating a coding agent means letting it install packages

insights.claim: Reward hacking, where an agent earns a passing score by tampering with tests or overwriting its score file, is a flagged risk, and network restriction removes one avenue of cheating but the post does not claim to prevent in-sandbox tampering.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Benchmark scores may be inflated by cheating even in isolated environments.

insights.claim: Harbor now runs each evaluation task in a Docker Sandbox microVM with its own kernel, so agent activity cannot reach the host or other tasks, and the same tasks run locally or in Docker Cloud Sandboxes.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: MicroVM isolation is becoming the standard for running untrusted agent code.
insights.locator: Each task runs in a Docker Sandbox, a microVM with its own kernel

insights.claim: Docker tested Harbor with 64 concurrent tasks on Cloud Sandboxes, with higher limits on request, but gave no data on startup overhead, per-task cost or eval score variance.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Teams must benchmark cost and latency themselves before committing.
insights.locator: The announcement does not include benchmark data on startup overhead

insights.claim: Cloud Sandboxes allow configurable network policies so tasks can pull dependencies in setup then restrict internet access, giving every agent identical network conditions, but local mode supports only public and no-network modes.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Fair, reproducible comparisons require the cloud path for fine-grained control.
insights.locator: In Docker Cloud Sandboxes, configurable network policies

insights.claim: Docker Compose support lets Harbor run multi-container tasks inside a single cloud sandbox with services and sidecars sharing one microVM.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo

insights.claim: The integration is in the nightly Docker Sandboxes release (Harbor pinned to 0.24.1.dev202610150414) with a stable release on October 23, uses the sbx extra and the -e sbx flag, and cloud runs need a Docker account with Cloud access and a personal access token.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Early adopters can test now; cloud usage ties into Docker's paid offering.
insights.locator: The integration is available now in the nightly release

insights.claim: Harbor supports sandbox providers including Daytona, Modal, E2B, Runloop, Tensorlake, LangSmith, Blaxel, Novita Sandbox, EC2 and Beam, with docs suggesting Daytona because it supports multi-container docker-compose deployments that Modal, E2B and Runloop lack.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Many vendors compete for the agent-execution sandbox layer; Docker is entering an established field.
insights.locator: On the Harbor side, the framework shows horizontal-scaling integrations

insights.claim: Docker is placing Sandboxes under other agent platforms: NanoClaw deploys in a Docker microVM, GitHub Agentic Workflows added Docker Sandboxes as a runtime in July 2026 (gh-aw 0.82.9), and the sandbox has its own Docker daemon so Testcontainers tests run without mounting the host socket.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Docker is positioning Sandboxes as default agent runtime infrastructure.
insights.locator: Beyond Harbor, Docker has been placing Sandboxes under other agent platforms

insights.claim: The September 24 Cloud Sandboxes launch lets agent workflows continue when a laptop shuts down, with reported one-hour default sessions, a 24-hour maximum, no compute charge for paused sandboxes, and Kits packaged as OCI images that Docker will submit to the CNCF.
insights.speaker: Claudio Masolo
insights.so_what: Pricing and session limits shape the economics of cloud agent execution.
insights.locator: The Harbor integration builds on the Cloud Sandboxes launch from September 24
